threshold_tuned_on: validation only, applied once to test

oscar_baseline.correction: earlier runs in this project compared npm against OSCAR Table 5(a) PyPI (0.99/0.85/0.91). That understated the npm gap by ~4 F1 points.

ceiling_analysis.note: 26% of malicious packages execute nothing during installation and are structurally undetectable by install-time behavioural monitoring

improvement_attempts.corrected_installer_bins: no change beyond noise (npm/node were counted as foreign binaries in every trace)
improvement_attempts.ancestry_and_node_exec_features: no change; redundant with existing shell/nettool counts. node-exec rule is 100% precision but only 5.5% recall
improvement_attempts.stack_with_gradient_boosting: WORSE (73.5-76.5% vs 79.28%). TGN/GBM score correlation 0.896 - no complementary signal. Blend tuned on val improved val (86.54%) but degraded test (76.47%), i.e. val overfitting
improvement_attempts.conclusion: ~79-80% F1 is the ceiling of install-time behavioural data on this corpus
improvement_attempts.stack_with_static_hook_content: WORSE (75.73% vs 79.28%). TGN/static correlation 0.856. Val improved (87.50%) while test degraded -- validation overfitting with n=272.

all_18_static_features_REJECTED.why_rejected: driven by corpus-shape artifacts, not malice. has_readme AUC 0.873 (benign 92% vs malware 17%), tar_bytes 619KB vs 280KB, n_files 66 vs 13, version_major 16 vs 24.4M. The malicious samples are throwaway PoC stubs; the benign are real published libraries. A real typosquat of a popular package ships a README, full source and a plausible version, so every one of these features inverts. Same failure mode as the /dev/pts artifact.

improvement_attempts.useful_byproduct: static hook-content alone gives 97.37% precision at 64.91% recall on test -- a viable high-confidence blocking mode.
improvement_attempts.final: TGN behavioural ensemble at 79.28% test F1 is the honest result. 90+ is not reachable on this dataset without corpus artifacts.

comparability_caveats: OSCAR and all Table 5(b) baselines score all 500 malicious packages; SCBF could only score the 379 that installed successfully (dynamic analysis requires execution).
SCBF test split holds 57 malicious samples -> roughly +/-4% on F1.
All baselines analyse the complete package (source, metadata, full install). SCBF decides from behaviour alone at event 1500, mid-install, and terminates the installer.

SPLIT_LEAK_BUG.what: train.py used --seed for BOTH model init AND the train/val/test split, so every ensemble member got a different partition. Scoring the ensemble on member-1 test set meant members 2 and 3 had trained on most of it.
SPLIT_LEAK_BUG.measured: 190/273 and 197/273 npm test packages were in a sibling member train set (145/210 for pip)
SPLIT_LEAK_BUG.fix: added --split-seed (fixed, default 42); --seed now controls model init only. Verified: 0 test packages in any member train/val.

scoped_note: the hook-declaring scoped evaluation (91.14%) was computed on the leaked models and is withdrawn; recompute on the clean ensemble if wanted

model_selection.why: the hybrid produces identical test predictions to the TGN alone, so the GBM stage adds an artifact and inference cost for no measured gain. TGN-only also has the higher test AUC.
model_selection.contrast_with_pypi: on PyPI the statistical features dominate (GBM alone 94.92% vs TGN 89.91%); on npm the TGN dominates. pip malware is visible in aggregate volume patterns, npm malware is a process-spawn sequence -- which is what the temporal graph model captures.

train_metrics_note: npm has no gradient-boosting stage, so these train figures reflect the neural ensemble and are interpretable (unlike PyPI, where the GBM memorises its training split). train->test F1 gap +3.84%; train recall 69.81% vs test 66.67% -- a data ceiling, not overfitting.
